title: Imagining Media
description: Introduction to the multiple media formats in contemporary society. Through creative assignments and analyses of creative work in various media platforms, students grow in their abilities to create, use, and appreciate contemporary media technologies and frameworks.
prerequisites: Restricted to first years, sophomores, and juniors.

title: Art of Film and Media
description: Introduction to the fundamental visual and audio techniques used in cinema, television, and emerging media to convey meaning and mood. Careful analysis of selected films, TV shows, and other media. Required of all majors.
prerequisites: Restricted to first-years, sophomores, and juniors.

title: Introduction to Screenwriting
description: Introduces the language of screenwriting. Topics include the creative process of idea generation and ways to make a story filmable; the creation of memorable and redeemable characters; the arc and transformation of story, including the setup, the question or conflict, the turning point, and the climax or ending; and the details of proper format and presentation. Required of all majors.

title: Introduction to Production
description: Practical, comprehensive course in the fundamentals of digital video and audio production, covering cameras, microphones, lighting, shooting, editing, sound design, and outputting. Incorporates hands-on exercises, screenings, lecture, and group and individual video projects. Required of all film and media arts majors.
prerequisites: Restricted to first years, sophomores, and juniors.

title: Film and Media Criticism
description: Introduces the various forms of written criticism of film, television, and digital media, including journalistic criticism, genre criticism, and auteur criticism. Also introduces the fundamentals of ideological and cultural criticism. Required of all FILM majors and International Film Studies minors.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1301. Restricted to FILM majors only, or International Film Studies minors who have completed one of the following courses: ARBC 2402, CHIN 2402, FREN 2302, GERM 2302, ITAL 2302, JAPN 2402, RUSS 2312, SPAN 2302.

title: Creativity and Ideation
description: This hybrid production and studies course on creativity in film and media examines the nature of creativity in different fields and businesses. Includes how creativity in film and media manifests both in finished works themselves and within the production process. Explores different sources of ideas and develops ways to generate a myriad of project pitches, stories, and concepts. Students leave the course with multiple ideas for potential projects for future production courses.

title: Screenwriting Formats
description: Students learn how to craft screenplays for diverse types of media production. Students develop multiple scripts across different genres and formats.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1300, ENGL 2390, or THEA 3331; and FILM 1303 or THEA 3332.

title: Production Formats
description: Exposure to the creation of diverse types of media production. Students work on multiple projects across the course through production and completion, with each project a different form of audiovisual media (e.g., music video, commercial, soundscape, experimental).
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1300 and FILM 1304.

title: History of Recorded Music
description: Connects major periods of recorded music to innovations in music hardware with special focus on the importance of music to the radio, television, cinema, and new media industries.

title: Screen Acting
description: Designed to help the director understand the actor’s process of crafting performances. Explores a basic overview of these techniques through monologue and scenes. Concentrates on the unique circumstances given to the single-camera film actor, including set etiquette, technical basics, blocking, and general camera awareness. Also addresses the marketing needed to secure acting jobs and careers.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Film & media arts or theatre majors.

title: American Popular Film and Television
description: An in-depth examination of specific aspects of American popular cinema and/or television, with a focus on questions of popular culture and ideology, the historical development of styles and genres, and the impact of the Hollywood film industry. Specific topics vary from term to term.

title: Contemporary Media Industries
description: Overview of the key cultural, technological, economic, and legal aspects of media industries today. Required of all majors.
prerequisites: Restricted to first-years, sophomores, and juniors.

title: History of Animated Film
description: Provides a critical and historical overview of the development of the animated film from its origins in the 19th century to the present.

title: America on Film
description: Historical survey of the representations of social identity categories in American film and media, with a particular focus on race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and physical ability.

title: Media Production Ethics and Representation
description: A production-based course on ethical and representational practices in media creation, with particular emphasis on diversity and inclusion relating to race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and physical ability. Also covers practical production ethics and procedures.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 1304.

title: History of Cinema and Tv Comedy
description: Survey of the development of comedy in film and television, with emphasis on a historical examination of comic films and TV shows. Also, a theoretical analysis of the phenomena of humor and laughter.

title: Film and Television Genres
description: Examines questions of genre pertinent to film and television by focusing on various generic forms and their history. Specific genres for consideration vary from term to term.

title: Experimental Camera
description: Pushing the technical boundaries of cameras as capture devices, students experiment with the creative aesthetic possibilities therein (still and/or motion) and then draw from a variety of genres to create short, experimental films. Students explore diverse concepts such as storytelling, portraiture, documentary, poetry, and abstraction, and they combine elements such as still photography, animation, graphics, narration, sound effects, and original music to create motion picture media. Students are required to have access to at least a digital still camera.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1304, or ASPH 1300 and ASPH 1310 (or instructor permission is available for students with a working knowledge of the camera, including aperture, shutter speed, and focal length), and a basic understanding of video editing.

title: Screenwriting for Television
description: Students produce a first draft of an episode to a television series. Review of proper format and the structure of beats and acts, as well as different television program formats, including series and serial television. Work includes step outlines of each act, scene readings, and collective feedback, culminating in a fully realized first-draft screenplay of an episode.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 2303.

title: Screenwriting for Feature Film
description: Students produce a first draft of a feature screenplay. Review of proper format and act structure leads to a more in-depth exploration of story, character, dialogue, scenes and scene sequencing, narrative devices, and the emotional payoff. Work includes step outlines of each act, scene readings, and collective feedback, culminating in a fully realized first-draft screenplay.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 2303.

title: Intermediate Production
description: Production course building on skills from FILM 1304 and FILM 2304, going deeper on both the creative and technical aspects of cinematography and sound design. Students build understanding of how to develop visual and aural designs that support and enhance their cinematic stories, and how to execute these designs using professional cameras, lighting, grip, and audio equipment, as well as professional color and sound design software.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 2304.

title: Producing
description: An overview of the basic business, legal, and logistical aspects of organizing and overseeing film and media production.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1303 and FILM 1304.

title: Documentary Production
description: Students explore and learn from various approaches to documentary filmmaking. Hands-on assignments, screenings, readings, lectures, and discussions prepare students to analyze and produce documentary films.

title: Editing
description: This course on the creative art and craft of editing develops storytelling and rhythmic sensibilities through close study of films, critique and discussion of works in progress, and hands-on practice. Projects include short editing exercises, reworks of students’ own existing projects, and re-edits of others’ films.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 1304.

title: Screen Artists
description: Examines the questions of authorship pertinent to the cinema by focusing on the works of one or more film artists. The specific directors, producers, screenwriters, and other artists treated by the course vary from term to term.

title: 16 MM Production
description: A focus on visual language and 16 mm film production techniques. Each student makes a short film, shooting only nonsynchronous original material. Covers use and operation of the Bolex 16 mm film camera: incident light meter, fixed focal length lenses, film speeds, and color temperature ratings. Also, visual design through effective lens choice, mise-en-scène, location usage, and production design. Students gain a deeper understanding of how to use visual language to express their ideas.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 1304.

title: Film Directing
description: Covers all elements of the directing process, with specific emphasis on how the film director works with screen actors and captures actors’ performances to fit the director’s vision. Students learn about script analysis, character outline, casting, rehearsals, and on-set direction.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1303 and FILM 1304.

title: Cinematography
description: Advanced production class focusing on the articulation of motion picture language through the technical and aesthetic concerns of the lens, composition, lighting, visual design, camera movement, and point of view. Students explore each of these elements in theory and in practice to better develop their visual storytelling skills. Examination and analysis of art, print media, films, videos, and TV shows is complemented by demonstration of and intensive hands-on practice with camera, lighting, grip, electric, filtration, modern color grading techniques, and software training.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 3304.

title: Film Exhibition and Distribution
description: Detailed examination of contemporary practices in the distribution and exhibition of theatrical feature films, including the roles of audience survey techniques, booking, publicity, and advertising.

title: Introduction to Animation
description: Studies in traditional animation principles, including squash and stretch, timing and spacing, morphing, paths of action, overlapping actions, walk/run cycles, balance, and jumping. This introduction to character animation, with class exercises in character acting in both voice and movement, helps students translate performance into their animated characters. Students have opportunities to work with multiple methods of animation, including 2-D traditional hand drawn, Claymation, stop motion, and 2-D/3-D CGI software.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 1304.

title: International Film History
description: Overview of the development of the cinema as a technology, an art form, an industry, and a social institution, beginning with the origins of the medium and tracing its major movements and configurations up to the present. Required of all film and media arts majors.
repeatability: Overview of the development of the cinema as a technology, an art form, an industry, and a social institution, beginning with the origins of the medium and tracing its major movements and configurations up to the present.

title: American Film History
description: An overview of U.S. film history from the silent period to the present day. Emphasis on the genres, directors, cinematic techniques, and industrial factors that advanced the art of Hollywood and independent filmmakers.

title: American Broadcast History
description: Focus on the history of American television, with an emphasis on the industrial and sociocultural aspects of the medium's development. Issues of race, gender, class, genre, sexuality, and national identity are studied in the context of significant television shows of the past and present.

title: History of Documentary Film and Television
description: An overview of the development of the documentary mode surveying historical and critical aspects of nonfiction cinema and TV, including newsreels, social issue films, propaganda movies, wartime documentaries, the cinema verité movement, network documentary series, and reality TV.

title: National Cinemas
description: Examines the social, economic, technological, and aesthetic histories of cinema from various nations. Also, the concept of “national cinema.” Specific nations for consideration vary from term to term.

title: Postwar European Cinema: 1945-Present
description: Presents an overview of postwar European cinema, with a focus on major films, directors, and national movements. Considers cultural and stylistic features that differ from Hollywood-genre models. (Summer abroad)

title: Sound
description: Comprehensive audio course with instruction and work in recording, editing, mixing, and design. Topics include microphone selection and placement, Pro Tools, advanced recording techniques, routing in a studio and within software, Foley sound effects, automated dialog replacement, and introduction to audio processors. Also, individual and group sound-design projects.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 1304, MSA 3310, or instructor permission.

title: Post-Production Visual FX
description: Project-based studies in design concepts and application to graphics and visual special FX. Introduces 3D design, compositing techniques, and motion tracking, including working with virtual cameras and lighting.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1304 and consent of instructor.

title: Topics in Production
description: Focus on a specific area of production. Subjects and prerequisites vary from term to term.

title: Topics in Postproduction
description: Focus on a specific topic of film/video postproduction. Subjects and prerequisites vary from term to term.

title: Topics in Screenwriting
description: An exploration of a particular genre or format of screenwriting. Topics vary each semester.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 2303.

title: Topics in Film and Media Studies
description: Focuses on a specific topic pertinent to film and media studies (e.g., film and/or television history, criticism, critical theory). Topics vary from term to term. May be repeated once with a different topic.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1301 or FILM 1302.
repeatability: May be repeated once with a different topic.

title: Topics in Media Industries
description: Focuses on a specific topic related to the business and/or industrial side of film and media. Subjects vary from term to term.

title: Gender and Sexuality in Media
description: Covers a range of issues related to gender and sexuality in film, television, and other media.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 1300 or FILM 1301.

title: Internship
description: Offers practical experience through work in the professional media, either part-time during the fall or spring terms, or full-time during summer. Students may take a maximum of 3 credit hours of internship (150 hours of work per term is calculated as 3 credit hours). Internship credit is given on a pass/fail basis only.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Permission of instructor and upper-division standing.

Students may take a maximum of 3 credit hours of internship (150 hours of work per term is calculated as 3 credit hours). Internship credit is given on a pass/fail basis only.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Permission of instructor and upper-division standing.

title: TV Ad Concepting and Production
description: Working collaboratively, students create and develop ideas for 30-second commercials for predetermined clients, complete all necessary preparation for producing these concepts, and shoot and edit them into finished ads. Focus is on real-world commercial-style production, emphasizing how to address clients’ specific needs while maintaining the creative elements of design and production. Completed ads are submitted to national and/or international advertising competitions and festivals. Note: Interdisciplinary course cross-listed with ADV 4397; usually offered during the January or summer term. Generally, students must have taken ADV 3395 and/or FILM 3304 beforehand, though in special cases exceptions may be made.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Instructor consent.

title: Screenwriting the Adaptation
description: Students learn the process of creating a screenplay based on work from another source. Issues covered include how to translate from one medium into another, how to condense original material, and the consideration of updating or otherwise adding original ideas into the adaptation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FILM 2303.

title: Advanced Production
description: Advanced-level production course building on the techniques and tools covered in FILM 1304, FILM 2304, and FILM 3304. All students work collaboratively to take short film projects through production and completion. Emphasizes using craft productively to create engaging, polished works.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 1303, FILM 2304, and FILM 3304.

Students may take a maximum of 3 credit hours of internship (150 hours of work per term is calculated as 3 credit hours). Internship credit is given on a pass/fail basis only.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Permission of instructor and upper-division standing.

title: Philosophy of Film and Media
description: Provides an overview of major philosophical and theoretical writings on cinema, television, and new media (including the work of theorists such as André Bazin, Sergei Eisenstein, Laura Mulvey, and Christian Metz) and demonstrates the application of various analytical perspectives to specific texts.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 3351 and one of FILM 2301, FILM 2362, or FILM 2363.

title: Directed Study
description: Independent study under the direction and supervision of a faculty member. A directed study is a close collaboration between the professor and an advanced student who conducts a rigorous project that goes beyond the experience available in course offerings.
prerequisites: The student must secure written permission from the instructor and return a completed directed studies form to the Film and Media Arts Office before the start of the term during which the study is to be undertaken. Prerequisites: Junior standing and permission of instructor.

title: Media Career Preparation Colloquium
description: Preparation for entrance into the media industries as a career, via guest presentations by industry professionals and in-class lectures on resume preparation, networking, and personal marketing strategies.
prerequisites: Corequisite: FILM 4225, FILM 5205, FILM 5213, or FILM 5214, or prerequisite: FILM 4225 or FILM 4325.

title: Production Thesis
description: Centered on completing a high-quality senior thesis film using classes as a workshop to improve projects in preproduction, production, and postproduction phases. Designed as the culmination of the production pathway curriculum, providing a forum for putting the ideas, skills, and techniques learned through the curriculum into use on one ambitious piece. The thesis project must ultimately be defended to and approved by a faculty committee.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 5305 and thesis proposal approval. Corequisite: FILM 5112.

title: Screenwriting Thesis
description: Centered on completing a high-quality senior thesis screenplay using classes as a workshop to improve and fine-tune a feature-length project, or a pilot episode and "bible" for a series. Designed as the culmination of the screenwriting pathway curriculum, providing a forum for putting the ideas, skills, and techniques learned through the curriculum into use on one ambitious piece. Enrolled students must come to class on the first day with a treatment and/or outline that has been pre-approved for acceptance into the course. The thesis screenplay must ultimately be defended to and approved by a faculty committee.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Approval of screenwriting thesis proposal. Corequisite: FILM 5112.

title: Research Thesis
description: An advanced critical studies course in which students research, write, and defend a research paper, 10,000-15,000 words in length developed in consultation with a faculty adviser. The thesis is designed to synthesize interests and works that the student may have developed in previous critical studies courses, and to potentially serve as an essay for scholarly publication or for application to a graduate program in media studies. While the course is individually structured and highly self-directed, it also requires regular meetings with the thesis adviser. The thesis must ultimately be defended to and approved by a faculty committee.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Thesis proposal approval. Corequisite: FILM 5112

title: Thesis Development
description: Capstone-level project workshop, designed to develop and work on senior thesis-level projects. Students must have a capstone plan in mind when they begin the course. If students have chosen the Screenwriting Emphasis, they should have a long-form (feature or series) script idea to develop; if they have chosen the Production Emphasis, they should choose either a short film project to direct (any form - scripted narrative, documentary, experimental, etc. - as long as it is of thesis scale/caliber) or a planned key creative craft role (cinematographer, sound designer, production designer, editor). By semester’s end projects will either be completed or have made solid progress (long-form script concepts and outlines are fleshed out; short film projects are through pre-production and principal photography). Projects still in-progress will be reviewed by faculty for approval to be completed in FILM 5205 or FILM 5213.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FILM 4304; or FILM 3302 and FILM 3303. Restricted to film and media arts B.F.A majors with senior standing only.

prerequisites: The student must secure written permission from the instructor and return a completed directed studies form to the Film and Media Arts Office before the start of the term during which the study is to be undertaken. Prerequisites: Junior standing and permission of instructor.

title: Media Career Preparation
description: Through various assignments, research, lectures, field trips, and guest presentations by industry professionals, students learn about career options and opportunities in the field of media arts. Students are expected to prepare for their short- and long-term career goals through research projects, the creation of personal marketing pieces (e.g., business cards, reels of their work, and film festival submissions), the preparation of appropriate résumés, networking, and the creation of a final project designed to launch their individual careers in the entertainment industry. Substantial work outside the class periods is required.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior standing. Restricted to film majors.

title: Critical Studies Seminar

title: Games and Global Society
description: This course examines the cultural, social, and economic impact of video games on a global scale. Students explore how games reflect and influence social interaction within a culture and across different cultures. Through case studies, readings, and interactive discussions, students analyze the ways games shape and are shaped by society, as well as the opportunities of creators in a global context. Students gain a deeper understanding of the societal significance of games and the skills to assess their role in contemporary culture.

title: Ludology
description: Students learn to apply methodologies of modern ludic theory in both the deconstruction and analysis of games and their systems, as well as the generation of innovative gameplay solutions. This course covers an array of topics that range from understanding forms of logic and reasoning to evaluating gameplay analytics in an effort to develop a framework for game design problem-solving.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Extended Reality Games
description: The art and technology of emerging communication in human virtual environment interaction (HVEI). Extended reality content designers explore how to tap into a form of haptic intelligence, placing technological sensory output interfaces where the body is kinesthetically linked to the felt body via proprioception human interfaces: visual, auditory, haptic, and locomotory displays; position tracking and mapping in order to immerse an audience in a continuously updated computer-generated synthetic environment.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Generative AI Content for Games
description: Explores the use of generative AI technologies to modify and iterate on game content. Students learn how to leverage AI tools for procedural art, narrative generation, and assisted code while understanding the technical, creative, and ethical considerations involved. Through hands-on projects and experiments, students integrate AI-driven content into playable prototypes, evaluate its impact on gameplay and player experience, and explore workflows that combine human creativity with AI augmentation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Technical Art I: Visual Effects
description: Introduces students to the principles of generating visual effects for games. Topics include GPU based simulation and baked assets using standard industry tools.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CRCP 1350.

title: Graphical User Interface
description: Introduces students to the UI/UX design for in-game interfaces. Topics include layout design, widget logic, interaction systems, and usability considerations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Technical Art II: Real-Time Rendering Pipelines
description: Introduces students to the structure, terminology, and core systems of a modern real-time rendering pipeline. Students gain foundational proficiency in importing assets and placing objects in a 3D real-time game engine. Topics include draw calls, LOD systems, lighting, and GPU performance considerations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: GAME 3350.

title: Technical Art III: Digital Costuming
description: This advanced technical art course focuses on the creation and integration of digital costumes for interactive 3D characters. Students explore the design, construction, and optimization of virtual garments using procedural modeling pipelines and industry-standard digital fashion tools. Emphasis is placed on translating artistic concepts into technically efficient assets that perform effectively within real-time game engines. Through a combination of design theory, simulation techniques, and practical implementation, students learn how to develop visually compelling and physically accurate costumes that enhance character identity and narrative immersion. The course also introduces advanced topics in deformation systems, rigging integration, and performance optimization for complex character assets. Students produce a final project demonstrating the full pipeline of digital costume design — from concept development to in-engine implementation — supported by research, critique, and iteration.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: GAME 3354.

title: Game Design
description: An intensive study designed to further integrate computational media and digital processes into creative practice. This course explores the fundamentals of game design. Students explore game design by analyzing and deconstructing videogames, critiquing serious games, and discussing current trends. It provides a foundational framework and language for discussion. The focus is on developing independent work, group collaboration, and analytical study applied to game design.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 3 credit hours of ASIM, ASDR, ASSC, ARHS, FILM, CRCP, ADV coursework, or instructor approval.

title: Monetization and Game Economy Design
description: Explores the design and implementation of in-game economies and monetization strategies in video games. Students analyze player behavior, virtual goods, reward systems, and revenue models to create engaging, balanced, and sustainable game economies. Topics include free-to-play mechanics, in-app purchases, progression systems, virtual currencies, and ethical considerations in monetization. Through case studies, hands-on exercises, and design projects, students learn to craft game economies that enhance player experience while achieving financial goals. Students are able to evaluate monetization strategies that are both player-centric and commercially viable.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Critical Issues
description: Students develop critical responses, dialogue, and write about videogames, art institutions, and other topics in games studies through student-led discussions on essays, lectures, and exhibitions by artists and critics.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 3 credit hours of ASIM, ASDR, ASSC, ARHS, FILM, CRCP, or ADV coursework, or instructor approval.

title: Advanced Studio I: Serious and Commercial Game Development Methodologies
description: A forum for game design majors in the third year of studies that facilitates the students’ ability to articulate their work using serious and/or commercial game development methodologies as artists and to defend and present it in a peer–group setting.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 3 credit hours of ASIM, ASDR, ASSC, ARHS, FILM, CRCP, or ADV coursework.

title: Indie Game Publishing
description: Equips students with the knowledge needed to bring independent games to market. Covering distribution platforms, marketing strategies, community building, legal considerations, and funding options, students learn the practical aspects of publishing and promoting games as an indie developer. Emphasis is placed on understanding the challenges and opportunities of the indie game ecosystem, from concept to release and post-launch support. Through case studies, hands-on projects, and industry insights, students have a deeper understanding of the historical significance of indie game development.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Professional Practice in Art
description: For game design majors in their final year of studies. A practical and informed approach to understanding the competencies that are required to sustain practice as an artist beyond the undergraduate experience. Students learn how to negotiate the professional aspects of art and to identify and take advantage of a host of opportunities. Topics include establishing a studio; applying for grants; exhibiting work; intellectual property law; the markets for videogames; and alternative models of production, distribution, and exchange of videogames. A submission of an artist statement is required.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: GAME 3390.

title: Advanced Studio II

title: Game Studio Entrepreneurship
description: Explores the foundational principles, strategies, and practical skills necessary to launch, manage, and grow a successful independent game studio. Students examine the business, creative, and operational aspects of game development, including funding models, team building, project management, intellectual property, marketing, and distribution. Through case studies, guest lectures from industry professionals, and hands-on studio simulations, students develop a business plan and strategic approach tailored to the unique challenges of the gaming industry. Students gain a deeper understanding of the entrepreneurial landscape of game development.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Cross-Disciplinary Teams
description: In this course, students learn the basics of collaboration across the diverse disciplines within a game development environment. Emphasizing communication, problem-solving, and creative integration, the course challenges students to work on small group projects with design, programming, art, and audio tasks. Through hands-on projects, students experience the dynamics of cross-disciplinary collaboration, understand the strengths and perspectives of different team roles, and develop strategies for resolving conflicts, coordinating workflows, and achieving cohesive game experiences. Students gain a deeper understanding of how they can contribute meaningfully to a collaborative game development project in both academic and professional settings.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DSIN 2350.

title: Game Development Incubator
description: This hands-on course immerses students in the end-to-end process of creating, prototyping, and launching original video games. Structured as an incubator, students work in teams to develop concepts, build playable prototypes, and iterate based on feedback, simulating the workflow of a professional game studio. Emphasis is placed on rapid development, creative problem-solving, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and real-world project management. Guest mentors and industry professionals provide guidance, critique, and insight into the challenges of bringing a game from concept to market. Student teams have a game prototype and the experience of working in a high-intensity, studio-like environment.
prerequisites: Restricted to incubator application acceptance.

title: Writing and Critical Reasoning
description: Teaches students to analyze arguments by employing high order critical thinking skills through a lens of culture journalism. Students learn to identify sound from faulty premises, detect logical fallacies, distinguish strong from weak conclusions, evaluate sources and become information literate. To demonstrate an understanding of the techniques of critical reasoning, students write essays, conduct research, and engage in a variety of additional university-level writing assignments. This course satisfies the CC Critical Reasoning (CR) Foundation requirement. Students who have already taken another course that fulfills the Critical Reasoning requirement cannot take this course.

description: Examines the importance of media literacy to modern democratic life, empowering students to become more critical consumers of news and digital content by teaching tactics and skills to detect bias, contemplate fairness and ethics, and verify claims and assertions. Credit is not allowed for both JOUR 2302 and JOUR 2303.

Students learn field production and editing, as well as broadcast writing and are exposed to studio and control room skills. This class requires a significant amount of work with multimedia production. Includes 3 hours of lecture and one 1.5-hour lab per week.

title: Sports, News Media, and Social Media Analytics
description: Students learn the evolving study of applied statistics in sports. Using a brief introduction to statistical theory and a history of sports statistics, students build on existing metrics to learn how to better explain critical trends within major sports. Computer-assisted methods are taught to help with acquiring data and discovering trends within the numbers to see what patterns can aid with storytelling. Students learn data visualization as an aid to storytelling and understand social media metrics to maximize engagement with audiences. Limited to journalism and applied physiology and sport management premajors and majors.

Students also create a digital portfolio to showcase their creative work. Includes 3 hours of lecture and one 1.5-hour lab per week.

title: Mass Media in Great Britain: Politics, Pin-Ups, and Propaganda
description: Explores the interaction between power, politics, and mass media in Great Britain; the history of the media in Great Britain; the health (or lack thereof) of mass media today and its impact on politics and popular culture; and how journalists report the news abroad and in the United States. Daily assignments include examination of newspapers and broadcast and Internet news available in the U.K. Students write papers based on visits to sites such as the British Library and the Imperial War Museum. British journalists, scholars, and foreign correspondents present guest lectures. Final class projects that include papers and class presentations involve group studies in specialized areas of British media. (SMU-in-London)

Students conceive, develop, and pitch an entrepreneurial idea while also learning the basics of freelancing and self-employment. Includes frequent visits from entrepreneurial journalists and guest speakers.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 2302 or JOUR 2303; sophomore standing.

prerequisites: Restricted to fashion media and journalism premajors, majors, and minors.

description: Introduces the diverse world of magazines. Students study exceptional magazine feature writing (profiles, narratives, analytical pieces, etc.) and practice feature magazine reporting and writing to prepare for professional work in the industry.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 2103, JOUR 2302, JOUR 2312. Restricted to majors and minors.

description: Intensive introduction to the art of generating original news ideas about issues of public significance; developing critical news judgment; unearthing often difficult-to-access information; and organizing the information into focused, well-documented, and compelling stories.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: JOUR 2313, JOUR 3362, JOUR 3370, or JOUR 3382. Restricted to journalism majors and minors.

title: Washington Term Internship

title: Podcasting
description: Students learn the basics of three different types of podcasting, from the basic question and answer interview to a longer narrative, storytelling podcast with multiple interviews on a focused topic. This course explores audio interviewing techniques, editing workflow, episode structure, writing, field and studio editing and mixing, as well as distribution and critical review. Students leave this class understanding the mechanics of how to produce, promote, and distribute various types of podcasts.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 2304, JOUR 2312, and JOUR 2314. Restricted to journalism majors and minors and fashion media majors only.

The goal is to teach communications majors to become more creative problem-solvers as professionals, and more critical as media consumers.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Sophomore standing.

prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 2103, JOUR 2302, and JOUR 2312. Restricted to fashion media and journalism majors and minors.

title: Media and Politics

prerequisites: Prerequisite: JOUR 2312.

title: Reporting on Human Rights
description: Students report and write publishable news articles about current human rights issues while analyzing the role U.S. and international media play in driving positive policy solutions through journalistic print and digital storytelling. Topics include the role of images in conveying the harsh truth of any human rights story, and the ways new media formats and shrinking budgets, etc. are changing the way journalists who cover these stories do their job.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: JOUR 2312. Restricted to fashion media and journalism majors and minors or instructor consent.

title: Advanced Video Journalism
description: Builds students’ skills in shooting and editing in a professional environment. Students produce video content for multimedia platforms, building compelling visual narratives using a combination of high quality video, interviews, still images, and natural and ambient sounds.

restrictions: Restricted to journalism majors and minors and fashion media majors only

description: Teaches principles and practices of photojournalistic/documentary/editorial storytelling for print, multimedia, and video contexts. Topics include features, portraits, lifestyle, product, and conceptual photography; picture story and essay production with attention to platform production. Explores principles and practices of visual storytelling including approach, theory, and ethics.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 2312 and JOUR 3357. Restricted to journalism majors and minors and fashion media majors only.
restrictions: Restricted to journalism majors and minors and fashion media majors only

title: Law and Ethics in a High-Tech World
description: Engages students in an in-depth examination of unresolved concerns regarding freedom of expression in the 21st century. Topics include digital copyright, privacy in the era of social media and virtual assistants, artificial intelligence, and hate speech. Course provides students the opportunity to examine topics of interest in depth and to develop both topical knowledge and critical thinking skills.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 4316 or CCPA 3300.

title: Broadcast II
description: Furthers the foundation established in JOUR 3385. The curriculum emphasizes deadline-driven, off-campus beat reporting and broadcast producing. Students learn how to plan original story ideas, including investigative and long-form pieces. Convergence laboratory required. JOUR 4300 is highly recommended before taking this course.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 2313 (or JOUR 3362, JOUR 3370, or JOUR 3382) and JOUR 3385. Restricted to journalism majors and minors.

title: Arts Beat

title: Student Media Leadership

Students profile current American correspondents who work in foreign countries, comparing their work to those of their contemporaries. Includes newsgathering assignments that encourage students to publish on matters of international interest.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: JOUR 2313, JOUR 3362, JOUR 3370, or JOUR 3382. Restricted to majors and minors.

Students profile specific regions, examining the historical, political, economic, cultural, ethnic, and even geographical differences, to better understand the issues that affect the struggle for freedom of the press.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Sophomore standing.

Includes 3 hours of lecture and one 1.5-hour lab per week.

title: Listening for Commercial Music Applications
description: Involves the study and practice of ear training as it relates to the identification, manipulation, and perception of audio elements as used in the production of commercial music. Provides a concentrated in-depth study utilizing exercises designed to develop specific listening skills in 5 key audio production areas: songwriting, arrangement, production, mixing, and mastering.

title: Analysis of Music Production
description: Provides a basic yet broad understanding of the function of a music producer in both artistic and music business environments. The goal is to provide a forum to discuss and demonstrate how the role of music producer is concentric to all decisions in defining and recording artistic endeavors as they exist within the marketplace or elsewhere. Whether working with a director in producing music for a film score, collaborating with a songwriter to define an expression, working with a composer to achieve an artistic vision, or understanding how an advertising agency needs musical help in order to sell a product, the music producer must be able to coordinate the procedure with the vision. Even when the music producer is also the artist, composer, recording engineer, and financier, they must step outside of all other roles to plan how the end result can best be achieved. By the end of the term, students have an understanding of the process through which any musical work can best be defined as a recording or live performance.

title: Introduction to Digital Audio Workstations
description: Presents the concepts of recording and mixing music and audio using computer-based digital audio workstations (DAWs). Course topics include, but are not limited to, digital audio basics, mixing techniques, software-based audio effects processors, and MIDI recording using virtual instruments.

title: Recording Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles and techniques of audio recording and music production. While centered on audio recording of instruments and vocals, topics include the physics of sound, audio cables and connections, audio signal flow, microphones, digital audio and computer-based recording systems, studio setup, monitoring, MIDI music production, and session management.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MIPS 1325.

title: Songwriting Laboratory

title: Songwriting
description: Development of songwriting knowledge and skills, including essential components of a song, basic song forms, multiple approaches to starting and completing songs, recording basics, and related aspects of music law. Does not satisfy the 3000-level or above MUTH requirement for music majors.

title: Audio Mixing and Post-Production
description: This hands-on course explores the essential principles of sound design, mixing, and audio finishing for film, television, and digital media. Students gain practical experience balancing sonic elements, cleaning up location audio, and utilizing advanced digital audio workstations to deliver broadcast-ready audio.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MIPS 2325.

The role of the music producer is concentric to all decisions in recording and defining artistic endeavors. Whether working with a director in producing music for a film score, collaborating with a songwriter to define an expression, working with a composer to achieve an artistic vision, or understanding how an advertising agency needs musical help in order to sell a product, the producer must be able to coordinate the procedure with the vision. Even when the producer is also the artist, composer, recording engineer, and financier, they must step outside of all other roles to plan how the end result can best be achieved.

description: Examines the wealth of the organ repertory in combination with aspects of the different styles in organ building from the Middle Ages to J.S. Bach. The historical contexts of individual compositions, analytical aspects and performance-related issues are discussed. An optional integrated Organ Study Tour (8-12 days) to varying destinations in Europe and the United States is integrated into the course.

title: Classical and Romantic Song Literature

Students prepare repertoire for performance in class and make presentations on topics of specialized interest. Lectures focus on specific developmental trends such as the genesis of the song cycle, the evolution of the piano accompaniment in the 19th century, and links between poets and composers.

Provides students with a general knowledge of the literature to acquaint them with performance and notational practices, and to develop the musical skills necessary to perform this literature.

description: An overview for singers of the great masses and oratorios of the 18th and 19th centuries, with an emphasis on performance. Baroque, Classical, and Romantic styles are taught through the study and performance of arias and ensembles from these works. Students are coached by the instructor, and they perform for the class.

title: Introduction to Music in World Societies
description: Introduces students to musics from a diverse range of cultures, in addition to themes and issues in contemporary musical research. The first portion of the course provides a general introduction to case studies of music traditions from around the world, highlighting the contexts of music production in cultural and geographic regions. The final portion of the course applies this cultural knowledge in analytical contexts to broader discussions of indigeneity, nationalism, diaspora, traditions, and globalization.

title: Introduction to Music in History and Culture
description: Designed to provide a big-picture overview of music’s role in varied historical and cultural contexts; to acquaint students with the central paradigms, methods, and problems of music scholarship; and to provide a critical orientation of some of the major philosophical questions that play a role in subsequent music history coursework at SMU. Questions to be addressed include: What is music? What is its purpose? What does music mean, how does it mean, and how is it able to move the emotions? How is music historically and culturally constituted? How do we study it? Students engage with these and many other questions through intensive reading, listening, and lecture. Examples are drawn liberally from Western art music and popular music.

title: Global Pop
description: Considers the global production and consumption of music and how popular music scenes and markets operate across the world. Studies how popular musics have emerged and the ways in which phenomena including globalization, economics, and new technologies have impacted musicians, musical practices, and identities. No previous musical experience is necessary.

title: From Cotton Fields to Concert Halls: The African-American Impulse in American Classical Music
description: Overview of the contributions of African-American classical composers and concert artists from the American Reconstruction period to the end of the 20th century. Following a timeline of American social and political flashpoints (the Great Migration, the emergence of black colleges and universities, the Civil Rights Movement, black power protests, et. al.), the course explores how the music of black classical artists helped to evolve the American musical landscape.

title: Introduction to Critical Music Studies
description: Introduces the skills of critical reasoning, research methods, and argumentative writing through the lens of music studies. As a global practice influenced by historical, cultural, social, religious, and political beliefs and systems, music is a prime vehicle for developing research questions that apply critical reasoning and related skills. Drawing on perspectives and practices from across various fields of music studies (historical musicology, ethnomusicology, music theory, music psychology, music sociology, etc.), students learn to build sound arguments, distinguish strong from weak conclusions, become information literate, and write clearly and effectively. No previous musical study or experience is necessary. This course satisfies the CC Critical Reasoning (CR) Foundation requirement. Students who have already taken another course that fulfills the Critical Reasoning requirement cannot take this course.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in WRTR 1312, WRTR 2303, or WRTR 2305 or appropriate transfer credit

title: Jazz: Tradition and Transformation
description: Bunk, Bird, Bix, Bags, and Trane. From blues to bop, street beat to free jazz. A study of the people and music from its African, Euro-American origins through the various art and popular forms of the 20th century.

title: Introduction to Church Music Studies
description: An introduction to the history, theology, and practices of Christian congregational musics, ranging from the hymnody of the Christian West to songs of the world church and contemporary expressions of church music. Students learn how to apply current methodologies in church music studies to the study of congregational music and musicking, as well as understand the connections between the study of church music, both historically and theologically, and current musical practices.

title: Survey of Opera History
description: A chronological survey of opera, beginning with a brief introduction to medieval and Renaissance precedents, followed by an in-depth presentation of selected Baroque and Classical masterworks. Explores the ways 19th-century Romantic opera synthesized music, literature, art, and elements of politics and culture. Also, investigates the musical language and dramatic substance of selected works from 20th-century operatic repertoire. Students spend a significant amount of time viewing operas on video and laser disc, and in certain cases making comparative studies of productions. Offered Fall semester of even-numbered years.

Attention is directed to the forms, compositional procedures, and orchestration devices employed by selected composers who reflect the various stylistic orientations within this time frame. Included are the vihuela and Baroque guitar, four-string Spanish guitar, and related literature. Emphasis is given to the evolution of the modern instrument and its repertoire.

The focus is primarily on American cinema, but examples from other traditions are drawn on as well. Offered spring semester of even years.

Also provides an overview of medical terminology and population needs; explores cultural and ethical issue; professional scope of practice; boundaries and contraindications; and issues in self-care.

title: Voice for the Stage 1
description: Employing body awareness, modified yoga positions, and a variety of isolated physical actions, students deepen their experience of breath, impulse, and vibration. This process of freeing the vocal mechanism allows students to practice ease and efficiency of vocal release and to begin to make acting choices that are self-revealing. Addresses general patterns of self-editing and an initial expansion of the actor’s range and flexibility in performance.

title: Voice for the Stage 2
description: Students continue to practice ease and efficiency of vocal release and deepen their ability to make acting choices that are self-revealing. Vocal power, flexibility, and efficiency are enhanced and refined. Includes an introduction to phonetic information and execution of detailed speech actions.

title: Movement 1
description: Teaches students to individuate internal energies of the body, to use these energies in movement and creation of precise statuary mime for the stage, and to begin to synthesize physical listening skills for ensemble acting. Skills taught include juggling, hatha yoga, corporal mime, illusionistic pantomime, t’ai chi ch’uan, and improvisation of mime pieces.

title: Movement 2
description: Increases students’ physical listening skills and practices these in unarmed stage combat. Skills taught include t’ui shou, chi sao, foil fencing (left and right), French sabre, kung fu animals, and conventions of unarmed stage combat.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: THEA 2307.

title: Theatre Movement for Nonmajors
description: Students develop beginning skills as an acrobat, a stage fighter, an imaginative physical improviser, and a deviser of physical stories and storytelling. This hands-on course helps the student find a process that can be used to create character or to broach any movement or physical challenge presented by a role for the stage, in a public-speaking situation, or in any part of life. Designed for nonmajors.

title: The Art of Acting
description: Basic work in acting, voice, and movement for the nonmajor. Relaxation, concentration, imagination, and the actor's exploration and use of the social world.

title: Movement Musical Theater Dance Styles 1
description: Designed to introduce students to a variety of dance styles commonly used in musical theatre. The course emphasizes the development of technical skills, stylistic versatility, and performance quality. Students explore ballet, jazz, tap, modern, and social dance techniques, applying these skills to musical theatre choreography.

title: Musical Theater Acting I
description: Focuses on the seamless integration of acting and singing. The course emphasizes the transition from spoken dialogue to song and explores the historical context of musical theatre pieces. Students engage in scene study, song analysis, and research projects to deepen their understanding and performance skills.

title: Movement – Musical Theater Dance Styles 2
description: Builds upon the foundational skills developed in Dance Styles 1. This course further explores diverse dance styles, enhancing technical proficiency, stylistic range, and performance skills. Students engage in advanced choreographic work and performance projects, focusing on integrating dance techniques with musical theatre performance.

title: Fashion History and Culture
description: Explores how and why people tell others who they are by what they wear. Also, the role of clothing in and reflection of various historical cultures, including the relationship between fashion, art, architecture, and the decorative arts of selected time periods. For majors and nonmajors.

title: Spectacle of Performance
description: Students learn to deconstruct spectacle and to analyze its influence upon themselves and society. Offers the opportunity to go backstage to experience firsthand how effects are achieved. Students are required to attend performances in a wide range of live venues and discuss what they observe, enabling them to view performance on a critical level. For majors and nonmajors.

title: Text Analysis
description: Aids the first-year student in the skills necessary to read a play as an actor, a director, a playwright, a designer, and a student of drama; as such, it is an essential foundation step in the major. Explores key styles and genres of dramatic literature and important texts in the development of theatre. Includes lecture and discussion, and assignments include reading, written papers, and text-based exercises. Guest lecturers from the faculty will provide perspective on different areas of theatre production.

title: Technical Drawing for the Theatre
description: Principles and practice in the techniques of drafting traditional and nontraditional types of stage scenery. Students learn how to prepare and present construction and detail drawings for use in a scene, prop, or electric shop.

title: Introduction to Stage Management
description: An exploration of the methods and techniques of theatrical stage management, including preproduction planning, scheduling, and conducting rehearsals and performances. Assignments are both theoretical and practical. Permission of instructor required for nonmajors and first-year students.

title: Theatre Technology 1: Lighting Mechanics
description: Introduces basic principles of stage lighting design, including the mechanics and optics of lighting instruments, electrical theory and practices, control systems, basic design concepts, and color theory. Controllable qualities of light are investigated and demonstrated through the student’s participation on a lighting crew for a production. Students are expected to provide appropriate materials as needed.

title: Theatre Technology 2: Costume Construction Techniques
description: Introduces basic costume patterning and construction methods. Covers draping, drafting, flat-patterning, terminology, equipment usage, and the skills necessary to the entire costuming process. Students are expected to provide appropriate materials as needed.

title: Theatre Technology 3: Stagecraft
description: Introduces the organization of the scene shop, tool maintenance and usage, construction techniques, technical drawing development, computer applications, rigging, and time and material budgeting. Includes class projects and work on Meadows stage productions. Students are expected to provide appropriate materials as needed.

title: Theatre Technology 4: Introduction to Theatrical Sound
description: Introduces the organization of the sound studio, maintenance and usage of equipment, recording techniques, and computer applications. Includes class projects and work on Meadows stage productions. Students are expected to provide appropriate materials as needed.

description: Students refine their ability to execute detailed speech actions and identify specific phonetic changes using the International Phonetic Alphabet. Vocal power, flexibility, and malleability are enhanced. The application of voice and speech actions to heightened language and stakes in a scene is practiced and refined.

title: Voice for the Stage 4
description: Vocal power, flexibility, and expressive capability are practiced in a variety of space configurations. Students refine their ability to execute detailed speech actions and identify specific phonetic changes using the phonetic alphabet. The application of voice and speech actions to accents and dialects is practiced and refined.

title: Musical Theater Acting 2
description: Focuses on the seamless integration of acting and singing. Students engage in scene study, song analysis, and research projects to deepen their understanding and performance skills.

title: Musical Theater Acting 3
description: Builds on the skills developed in Musical Theater Acting 2. This advanced course focuses on complex scene work, historical analysis, and integrating advanced acting techniques with musical performance. Students explore character development, historical styles, and professional audition techniques.

title: Acting for Singers and Dancers
description: Advanced work in acting, voice, and movement built upon the foundational performance and presentation skills required for singing and dancing. Focus is on scene study intended to reinforce the actor’s development of a method of text analysis as an entry to a tactical approach (objective, obstacle, action) to acting and to facilitate the integration of text analysis and self-use as a process to create an emotionally honest, powerful, and effective moment of dramatic action on the stage. For dance majors and music vocal performance majors only.

title: Introduction to Design for the Theatre

title: Playwriting 1
description: Creative exploration in the development of performance scripts with emphasis on structural vocabularies of story, plot, character development, and dramatic action.

title: Playwriting 2

prerequisites: Prerequisite: THEA 3331.

title: Directing 1
description: Students research the relationship between a designer and director, and create and conceptualize various approaches to texts to gain a working vocabulary in the collaborative language among theatre artists. Culminates in a director and designer presentation or performance.

title: Directing 2
description: Production styles and methodologies evidenced in the art of major modern directorial innovators. Directing projects required.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: THEA 3341 and permission of instructor.

title: Textiles
description: Explores various fabrics and materials used in costume construction, millinery, and crafts for theatre and film. description: An exploration of the tools for computer image creation (e.g., AutoCAD, MiniCAD, and Adobe Photoshop) and their application.

title: Theatre and Drama History 1
description: Examines key moments in the history of Western theatre and drama. Focuses on selected dramatic texts and their social and cultural contexts, and to the dynamic interactions and changing relationships among performance, audience, and society as influenced by the advent of actors, playwrights, designers, and directors, and by changes in theatre architecture and the social definition of space.

title: Theatre and Drama History 2
description: Examines key moments in the history of Western theatre and drama. title: Studies in Theatre, Drama and Performance: Festival, Protest and Theatre
description: Explores the ways in which the conventions and practices of theatre and performance have informed and shaped events framed as public festivals and protests. Using the disciplines of literary criticism, theatre history, and performance studies, the class uses discussion, lecture, site visits, and student group/solo presentations to explore potential topics both historic and global. Readings and discussions examine the politics, aesthetics, and logistics of included events.

title: Studies in Theatre, Drama, and Performance
description: An examination of selected topics in theatre, drama, and performance. Texts, topics, and critical approaches vary.

title: Studies in Theatre, Drama & Performance: English Theatre in Context
description: Combining the academic disciplines of theatre history, gender studies, performance studies, urban studies, and literature, this course examines the complex relationship between the United Kingdom and the art/practice of live performance. With its focus on British theatre from Shakespeare’s time to the present, the course enables students to develop an awareness of the connection between the city and its theatre “landscape” through first-hand experience and in-class discussion. Students will attend performances, visit museums, exhibitions, and historic sites, and become familiar with London’s geography as part of this course.
